Unpaid work and family planning: read the daily average before assigning a 168-hour week

Five charts separate all-person and participant daily time averages, daily participation, an exclusive weekly schedule and an independently quoted four-week service budget.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Keep a fictional weekly time plan separate from its independently quoted cash cost

Interactive planning lab

Signed unassigned hours in the after-scenario week26.0
Change in unassigned hours from the before scenario4.0
Cash left after the quoted help over four weeks$320

Two fixed official source charts describe 2022 Time Use Survey daily person estimates, released 5 June 2024 and reviewed 25 October 2026. All-person daily means and activity-specific participant means have different denominators; daily participation is not past-year caregiver participation. These observations do not populate the controls. The final three figures are independent invented time and cash plans. The time model assigns exclusive non-overlapping blocks within one person’s 168-hour week: a fixed 71 hours for sleep, personal and other commitments, work/travel, and own domestic/care time. The 71-hour block is a teaching assumption, not a sleep, health or care standard. Before/after own-time inputs are separately assumed; a quote does not determine their difference. Negative remaining hours mean an overscheduled request, not a physically feasible week. Unassigned time does not establish usable leisure or paid-work capacity. The cash model compares four repeated weekly budgets with four total service invoices, rounding cash inputs to cents. Four weeks is not an average calendar month; receipt/invoice dates are not modeled. No provider-hour conversion, unpaid-work wage, additional earnings, benefits, taxes, borrowing or care-suitability conclusion is inferred.

The central idea

Time averages describe a defined population and day. A household plan needs its own exclusive time blocks and actual cash costs; a paid-help quote does not establish how many personal hours it frees.

01

Ask who is included in the daily time average

The 2022 Time Use Survey table reports 2.1 hours a day of unpaid household work across the full selected population, compared with 3.0 hours among people who performed that activity on their reference day. Both figures can be correct because their denominators differ.

The all-person mean includes people who recorded zero time in that activity that day. The participant mean conditions on doing it. A participant in adult care is not automatically a participant in child care, shopping or household work, so the participant population changes between rows.

For child care of people under 18 in the household or family, the published figures are 0.5 hours across the selected population and 3.4 hours among that day’s participants. These do not say every adult performs 3.4 hours of child care daily. The first chart keeps the two measures paired and explicitly labels their different bases.

02

Keep daily participation separate from care provided over a year

The companion measure is the share of persons performing the activity on the reference day. For the four plotted groups, the published percentages are household work 71.4%, child care 16.2%, adult care 3.9% and shopping 25.9%. A person can appear in more than one group, so these are not exclusive slices that must sum to 100%.

The reference-day denominator differs from reporting unpaid care at any time over twelve months. The existing caregiving cash-plan guide uses that separate participation context. Mixing the two survey concepts would turn a difference in measurement into an unsupported comparison of how common care is.

An invented arithmetic example makes the means easier to read. If three of ten people record four hours each and seven record zero, total time is twelve hours. The population mean is 1.2 hours, the participant mean is four hours and participation is 30%. With consistent unrounded quantities, 30% × four equals 1.2.

Published figures are independently rounded, so the displayed rates and means need not reproduce that identity exactly. Do not replace a published value with a product of two other rounded values. None of the three measures identifies a personal care need or a recommended daily workload.

03

Preserve the survey year, coverage and published precision

The table was released on 5 June 2024 and currently contains reference year 2022. Collection ran from 16 July 2022 through 15 July 2023. This article reviewed the current source on 25 October 2026. The figures describe the 2022 survey cycle, not a measured 2026 household week.

The selection is Canada, total persons aged 15 and over, and total all persons in the gender dimension. The survey metadata covers non-institutionalized people living off First Nations reserves in the ten provinces; the territories are outside the coverage. One selected person responded for the diary, rather than a proxy reporting every member’s schedule.

The source supplies 95% confidence intervals. The participation chart plots its published bounds, while this table retains the hour estimates and their bounds. A displayed interval of 0.1 to 0.1 reflects one-decimal rounding, rather than certainty about everyone’s time. The selected rows have blank status and symbol fields; no A/B/C grade has been invented.

The table’s “Unpaid work activities” aggregate includes household work, household/family child and adult care, and shopping. It reports population/participant means of 3.2/4.0 hours and daily participation of 79.1%. The separately listed outside-household help, community work and volunteering category is not part of that aggregate. Do not add a parent to its components or relabel every unpaid activity as dependent care.

04

A main-activity diary cannot describe every simultaneous responsibility

The official diary instructions describe a designated twenty-four-hour period from 4 a.m. to 4 a.m. the following morning. Assigned reference days help represent different days of the week. A reported day is not necessarily the respondent’s usual or preferred routine.

The official methods discussion distinguishes main activities, simultaneous activities and time spent with other people. It explains that exact simultaneous-activity duration was not collected and that primary child-care time can miss supervision and interaction. These published means therefore cannot reconstruct all time spent responsible for someone else.

The hypothetical weekly schedule below deliberately uses exclusive blocks so each clock hour is assigned once. That is a limited bookkeeping exercise, rather than a claim that real care duties never overlap work, travel or personal activities. An apparently unassigned hour can still involve a responsibility the small ledger does not capture.

05

Build the 168-hour plan from independently entered blocks

One person has 168 clock hours in seven days. The invented ledger assigns a fixed 71 hours to sleep, personal activities and other commitments, then adds requested work/travel and own domestic/care blocks. The fixed amount is a teaching assumption, not a health, sleep or care standard.

At the defaults, work plus travel takes 45 hours. Own domestic/care time is separately entered as 30 hours before an assumed arrangement and 26 hours after. Assigned time is 146 hours before and 142 after, leaving 22 and 26 hours unassigned. The signed bars compare the two remainders, and the waterfall reconciles the after scenario to 168.

The four-hour difference comes entirely from the chosen own-time assumptions. The calculator does not derive it from a provider’s invoice, service duration or a survey mean. The after figure can exceed the before figure if an arrangement adds coordination or other personal time. Each input needs its own evidence when a real plan is reviewed.

“Unassigned” means absent from the entered blocks. It does not prove that those hours are usable leisure, available paid work or adequate recovery time. A full plan may need further blocks, a different fixed amount or a dated schedule that this small example does not provide.

06

Retain a negative remainder instead of drawing an impossible schedule

If work and travel rise to 80 hours while the after domestic/care block stays at 26, the requested total becomes 71 + 80 + 26 = 177 hours. The remaining amount is negative nine hours. The calculator keeps that sign visible as an overscheduled request.

It does not squeeze 177 exclusive hours into a 168-hour donut, cap one category without saying so, or assume sleep or care can safely be cut. The negative number identifies a conflict in the entered exclusive plan. Resolving it requires actual facts about obligations and overlap, rather than a mathematical normalization.

Likewise, a four-hour increase in unassigned time is a difference between scenarios, not four extra hours added to the week. Total clock time remains 168. This time constraint is distinct from the cash constraint: a plan can have enough cash while its exclusive time requests still conflict.

07

Price the paid service separately from the time assumption

The cash controls use an independent total service quote of CAD 120 per week and CAD 200 per week available after other budget commitments. Over exactly four weeks, available cash is CAD 800 and quoted invoices total CAD 480, leaving CAD 320. Each week’s CAD 200 is a distinct budget amount; the same opening cash balance must not be counted four times.

Four weeks is a selected twenty-eight-day window. It is not an average calendar month, and the calculator does not silently use four weeks for every month of a year. It also does not determine whether each receipt arrives before the corresponding invoice. A dated cash calendar may reveal an additional timing need.

Changing the quote to CAD 250 per week raises four invoices to CAD 1,000, leaving an unfunded CAD 200 against the same CAD 800. Every time result stays unchanged. Conversely, changing own hours after the arrangement changes the time plan while leaving the quoted cost unchanged.

No unpaid-hour-times-wage calculation appears. The service quote supplies a cash amount, not a value for every hour of unpaid work, an income replacement, additional earnings or a guaranteed number of personal hours freed. Money independently available is entered directly; it is not inferred from work/travel hours or assumed to increase when unassigned time rises.

08

Review time and cash as separate constraints

For the official charts, retain the reference-day definition, population/participant denominator, age coverage, units and uncertainty. For a household plan, review the actual exclusive time blocks, simultaneous responsibilities, quoted service scope and dated payments. The public survey does not decide whether a particular arrangement meets care needs.

The tool does not model taxes, benefits, extra wages, borrowing, investment returns or an assessment of care suitability. A negative cash remainder represents missing funding rather than access to credit. A negative time remainder represents incompatible exclusive requests rather than a medical or safety diagnosis.

A useful planning statement keeps both quantities visible: “This assumed arrangement leaves 26 unassigned hours in the small weekly ledger and CAD 320 after four invoices, while the actual time change and service suitability still require verification.” That separates a transparent calculation from claims its inputs cannot establish.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
